113.title: The fingers will testify
113.hook: the Prophet ﷺ counted praises on his fingers, saying they'd be asked and made to speak (Tirmidhi)
113.howItsDone: After the prayer and through the day, many Muslims count short phrases of remembrance on the joints of the fingers of the right hand, following the Prophet's example; others use prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fajr, takbir to taslim. Your line was the whole thing. Did you catch the gray sky at dawn? Day one hundred thirteen.

A man sits after the prayer is done. His right hand rests on his knee, palm up. His thumb moves slowly from one finger joint to the next, and his lips move without sound. He isn't fidgeting. He's counting. The same hand, earlier in the day, typed, scrolled, held a cup, maybe tapped a car horn harder than it needed to. Now it's keeping a different kind of record. And the reason for counting this way, on the fingers, is a little startling. Today: the fingers will testify.
screen: `A THUMB MOVING JOINT TO JOINT.` → `HE'S COUNTING.` → `A DIFFERENT KIND OF RECORD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the prayer. This week opens what comes after it: dhikr, remembrance, the short phrases repeated after the prayer and through the day. And it starts with how they're counted. A hadith in the collection of at-Tirmidhi comes from a woman named Yusayrah, one of the early emigrants. She said the Prophet ﷺ told the women: hold on to glorifying God, and declaring His oneness and holiness, and count on your fingertips, for they will be asked, and made to speak. And don't be heedless, or you'll forget mercy. Asked and made to speak. It echoes the Qur'an. In Surah Ya Sin, it describes the Day of Judgment: mouths are sealed, and hands speak, and feet bear witness to what they earned. Read alone, it sounds like a warning: the body will tell what it did. Set beside this hadith, it can be heard another way. If the fingers will testify anyway, give them something good to say. Let them have counted glory. Another companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, said he saw the Prophet count his praises on his right hand. A common way today is the thumb touching each joint in turn, three on each finger, fifteen on one hand. Prayer beads are used too, and scholars have discussed them, but the reports themselves speak of fingers. Fingers are always with you. You can't leave them at home. And in the hadith's picture, the fingers that counted will one day speak of it.
screen: `THIS WEEK: DHIKR, REMEMBRANCE.` · `COUNT ON YOUR FINGERTIPS.` · `ASKED, AND MADE TO SPEAK.` · `GIVE THEM SOMETHING GOOD TO SAY.` · then, large: `THEY'RE ALWAYS WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten on your right hand. Rest the hand, palm up. With your thumb, touch the lowest joint of your little finger. One. The middle joint. Two. The tip. Three. Then the ring finger, three more. Then the middle finger. Keep going until you reach ten. If you pray, you can say a short phrase of remembrance on each count, like subhanallah. If not, just say the numbers, slowly, and feel each joint. Then let the hand rest open. The bell holds the time.
The fingers will testify. Count your praises on your fingertips, the Prophet said, for they'll be asked and made to speak. Today's word.
Your line: the fingers remember. Once today, when your hand reaches for your phone for no reason, touch three finger joints instead, and count. Day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: Subhanallah, thirty-three
114.hook: glory be to Allah, for what is beyond everything
114.howItsDone: After the obligatory prayers many Muslims say subhanallah thirty-three times, then alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar, counting on the fingers or on prayer beads, and they say subhanallah through the day at anything awe-inspiring.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fingers will testify, count your praises on your fingertips. Your line was the fingers remember. Did you touch three finger joints instead of reaching for your phone? Day one hundred fourteen.

A sunset over the water, and someone on the sand whispers: subhanallah. A baby's tiny hand closes around a finger: subhanallah. A crazy coincidence, a near-miss on the highway, a mountain out of a plane window. It's the word Muslims reach for when something is too big, too beautiful or too strange for ordinary words. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim sets it after every prayer, thirty-three times, counted out quietly. Today: the first of the three phrases, and what it's really saying.
screen: `A SUNSET, A BABY'S HAND.` → `TOO BIG FOR ORDINARY WORDS.` → `THIRTY-THREE, AFTER EVERY PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Subhanallah means glory be to Allah, and saying it is called tasbih. The root underneath, s-b-h, is the one the Qur'an uses for the sun and moon, each floating in its orbit. Some readers hear that picture inside the word: something moving far off, out of reach. The classical meaning is simpler and bigger: subhanallah declares God far above any flaw, any limit, anything a person could imagine. That's why it fits the sunset. The sunset is beautiful, and the One behind it is beyond even that. The Qur'an says, in Surah al-Isra, that the seven heavens and the earth and everything in them glorify Him, and there's nothing that doesn't hymn His praise, but people don't understand their glorifying. So in the tradition, the whole world is already saying subhanallah. The one praying is just joining in. After the prayer, there's a set. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says: whoever glorifies Allah thirty-three times after every prayer, and praises Him thirty-three times, and says Allahu akbar thirty-three times, and completes the hundred with there is no god but Allah alone, has their sins forgiven, even if they were like the foam on the sea. Tasbih is the first thirty-three. And one more thing. A string of prayer beads is often called a tasbih, too. The object is named after the word it counts.
screen: `A ROOT THE QUR'AN USES FOR ORBITS.` · `FAR ABOVE ANY FLAW.` · `THE HEAVENS ALREADY SAY IT.` · `THIRTY-THREE, THEN THIRTY-THREE.` · then, large: `THE BEADS ARE NAMED FOR THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thirty-three on your fingers. Rest your right hand, palm up. Touch each joint with your thumb, one count each. Fifteen joints makes one pass through the hand; go twice, and add three. If you pray, say subhanallah on each count, softly, not rushing. If not, say the word glory, or simply count, and on each count picture something beautiful you've seen this week. When you reach thirty-three, let the hand rest. The bell holds the time.
Tasbih. Saying subhanallah, glory be to Allah, far above anything; thirty-three times after the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: glory. The next time something stops you, a sky, a face, a kindness, don't reach for your camera first. Say the one word. Day one hundred fourteen.

115.title: Alhamdulillah, thirty-three
115.hook: all praise to Allah, for what is given
115.howItsDone: After each prayer, many Muslims say alhamdulillah thirty-three times following thirty-three subhanallah, and through the day they say it after eating, drinking, sneezing, and when asked how they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tasbih, subhanallah, glory be to Allah, far above any flaw. Your line was glory. Did something stop you, and did you say the one word? Day one hundred fifteen.

Day three, a long way back now, opened a word that comes out like a reflex. A meal finished: alhamdulillah. A sneeze: alhamdulillah. A friend asked how she's doing: alhamdulillah. The car starting on a cold morning: alhamdulillah. Back then it was a reflex, a word said once and gone. Today it comes back as a count. Thirty-three times, after the prayer, right after the glory. Saying it once without thinking is one thing. Sitting down to say it thirty-three times is another: the list has to keep finding things. Today: the praise.
screen: `BACK ON DAY THREE.` → `A REFLEX, THEN A COUNT.` → `THE LIST HAS TO KEEP FINDING THINGS.`

segments.voice: Alhamdulillah means all praise is for Allah, and saying it is called tahmid. Day three opened the root, h-m-d, and the line Arabic draws between praise and thanks. Today is about two other things: where the word sits, and what the tradition says it weighs. Start with where it sits. It's the opening line of the Fatiha, right after the bismillah: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. The Fatiha is recited in every rak'ah of every prayer, so by the time anyone reaches the count afterward, they've already said it more than once. Then the weight. A hadith in Sahih Muslim, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari, says: alhamdulillah fills the scale. And subhanallah and alhamdulillah, together, fill what's between the heavens and the earth. In the tradition's picture of judgment, deeds are weighed, and this one word fills the pan. Then the smallest version. Another hadith in Muslim says Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it. No great deed. A plate, a cup, and the word. Put those two side by side and the picture is a little strange: the word that fills the scale is the same word said over a glass of water. The thirty-three after the prayer sits between them. Some people use the count as a list, one thing for each joint of the fingers. The obvious things come first. Then the smaller ones: hot water this morning, a door someone held, a knee that didn't ache today.
screen: `ALHAMDULILLAH — ALL PRAISE IS ALLAH'S.` · `IN EVERY RAK'AH, IN THE FATIHA.` · `IT FILLS THE SCALE.` · `A MEAL, A DRINK, AND THE WORD.` · then, large: `ONE THING FOR EACH COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thirty-three on your fingers, with a thing for each. Rest your right hand, palm up. On each joint, name one thing, silently: a person, a meal, a bed, a body that works, a morning. If you pray, say alhamdulillah after each one. If not, say thanks, or just name it. If the things get smaller as you go, let them. Keep going to thirty-three. The bell holds the time.
Tahmid. Saying alhamdulillah, all praise is for Allah, the word that fills the scale; thirty-three after the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: thanks, again. At your next meal and your next drink, say it before the first bite and after the last sip. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: Allahu akbar, thirty-four
116.hook: the Prophet ﷺ taught this set to his daughter Fatimah instead of a servant (Bukhari)
116.howItsDone: Many Muslims say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, with subhanallah and alhamdulillah thirty-three times each, when going to bed, following the set taught to Fatimah, and a similar hundred after the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tahmid, alhamdulillah, the word that fills the scale. Your line was thanks, again. Did you say it before the first bite and after the last sip? Day one hundred sixteen.

Think of the most tired you've ever been from work with your hands. Moving house. A double shift. A newborn at three in the morning. Now picture a young woman in Medina whose hands are blistered from turning a stone hand mill every day, grinding grain for bread, and hauling water. She's the Prophet's ﷺ youngest daughter, Fatimah. She hears that some servants have come to Medina, and she goes to her father to ask for one. Just one. Someone to help. Today: what he gave her instead.
screen: `BLISTERED HANDS.` → `A STONE HAND MILL.` → `SHE ASKS FOR ONE SERVANT.`

segments.voice: The story is in Bukhari and Muslim, told by her husband Ali. Fatimah went to the Prophet's house, but he wasn't there, so she told his wife Aisha why she'd come. Later that night, after Fatimah and Ali had already gone to bed, the Prophet came to their house. They started to get up, and he said: stay where you are. And he sat down between them. Ali remembered feeling the coolness of his feet. Then he said: shall I tell you something better than what you asked for? When you go to bed, say Allahu akbar thirty-four times, subhanallah thirty-three times, and alhamdulillah thirty-three times. That is better for you than a servant. A hundred in all. It's a strange answer, if you're tired. She asked for help with the work, and he gave her words. But look at what the words are. Allahu akbar: God is greater. Greater than the mill, greater than the tiredness, greater than whatever the day took out of you. And he didn't send it with a messenger. He came himself, at night, and sat down on the edge of their bed to teach them. Ali said later that he never stopped saying it, not one night, even in the middle of a war. So the set that closes many Muslims' prayers, thirty-three, thirty-three, thirty-three or thirty-four, has a family story inside it. A tired daughter. A father at the bedside. A gift that doesn't wear out, and costs nothing, and is always there when the servant isn't.
screen: `FATIMAH ASKS FOR A SERVANT.` · `HE SITS DOWN BETWEEN THEM.` · `SOMETHING BETTER THAN WHAT YOU ASKED.` · `34, 33, 33, AT BEDTIME.` · then, large: `BETTER FOR YOU THAN A SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the full hundred. If you've just prayed, or whenever you can sit for two minutes, rest your right hand, palm up. Thirty-three of subhanallah, glory. Thirty-three of alhamdulillah, praise. Thirty-four of Allahu akbar, greater. Count on your finger joints, twice around the hand and a little more for each. If you don't pray, count the numbers, and on the last set, think of the thing that tired you most this week, and hold it next to the words. The bell holds the time.
Allahu akbar. God is greater, thirty-four times, the last of the three, the gift given to Fatimah instead of a servant. Today's word.
Your line: better than a servant. Tonight, when you lie down tired, try the hundred before you sleep, the way Fatimah was taught. Day one hundred sixteen.

117.title: La ilaha illallah
117.hook: the heaviest words on the scale, no god but Allah
117.howItsDone: Muslims say la ilaha illallah as dhikr after prayers and through the day, often counted on the fingers or beads, and hope it will be the last words on their lips before death.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Allahu akbar, thirty-four, the gift to Fatimah. Your line was better than a servant. Did you try the hundred before you slept? Day one hundred seventeen.

A scale, the old kind, two pans hanging from a beam. On one side: ninety-nine scrolls. Each scroll is a record of things they did wrong, and each one, the story says, stretches as far as the eye can see. The pan crashes down. On the other side, someone places one small card. A few words written on it. And the scale swings the other way. The scrolls fly up. The card is heavier. This is a hadith, in the collection of at-Tirmidhi. Today: the words on the card.
screen: `NINETY-NINE SCROLLS.` → `ONE SMALL CARD.` → `THE CARD IS HEAVIER.`

segments.voice: On the card is the testimony of faith, and its heart is the first half: la ilaha illallah. There is no god but Allah. Saying them is called tahlil. You've met them already, inside the shahada, the first pillar, and in the call to prayer, and at the end of the hundred after the prayer, three days ago. But look at how the sentence is built. It starts with a no. La ilaha: there is no god. Everything is cleared away first. Every idol. Some teachers read it more widely, too: anything a person serves without calling it worship, like money or approval. Nothing left standing. And then, illallah: except Allah. Only one thing comes back. Scholars call these two halves the negation and the affirmation. You empty the room, then let one in. The Qur'an puts the same idea in Surah al-Ikhlas, four short verses, which in Pickthall's translation reads: "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." A hadith in Tirmidhi calls la ilaha illallah the best remembrance. And a hadith in Abu Dawud says that whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah will enter Paradise. And that's the point of the card on the scale. Ninety-nine scrolls of mistakes, and one sentence that says, underneath all of them, I knew there was only one. In the tradition, that sentence, meant truly, weighs more than all the rest.
screen: `TAHLIL — NO GOD BUT ALLAH.` · `FIRST, A NO.` · `THEN ONE COMES BACK.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE.` · then, large: `THE CARD OUTWEIGHS THE SCROLLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it ten times, slowly, with the no and the yes. On la ilaha, breathe out, and let something go: one thing that takes up more of your mind than it should. On illallah, breathe in. Count on your fingers. If you pray, say the Arabic. If you don't, you can simply breathe the shape of it: out, letting go; in, one thing left. Ten times. Then rest the hand and stay quiet. The bell holds the time.
Tahlil. Saying la ilaha illallah, there is no god but Allah: a no that clears the room, and a yes. Today's word.
Your line: there is only one. When something today starts to feel like the only thing that matters, notice it, and put it back in its place. Day one hundred seventeen.

118.title: Astaghfirullah, a hundred times
118.hook: asking forgiveness a hundred times a day, as he did (Muslim)
118.howItsDone: Muslims say astaghfirullah three times right after finishing each prayer, and many repeat it through the day, sometimes a hundred times, following the Prophet's example.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tahlil, la ilaha illallah, the card that outweighs the scrolls. Your line was there is only one. Did you put something back in its place? Day one hundred eighteen.

How many times did you say sorry yesterday? Maybe a dozen. Sorry, bumped your cart. Sorry, running late. Sorry, can you say that again? Most of those sorrys aren't really apologies. They're just grease on the gears of the day. Now think about how many times you really asked to be forgiven for something. Maybe once. Maybe not at all. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ tells the people: O people, turn to Allah in repentance, for I turn to Him a hundred times a day. A hundred. Today: the word for asking forgiveness.
screen: `A DOZEN SORRYS A DAY.` → `HOW MANY REAL ONES?` → `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: The word is astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness. Saying it is called istighfar. The root, gh-f-r, means to cover, to shield. Arabic dictionaries list a soldier's helmet, mighfar, from the same root. So forgiveness, in this picture, isn't just wiping a slate. It's being covered, protected, from what the mistake would otherwise do. Now, the surprising part. Muslims generally hold that the Prophet was protected from serious sin, though the schools describe that protection differently. So why would he ask forgiveness a hundred times a day? The scholars give a few answers. Some say it's humility: the closer a person is to God, the more they notice the distance. Some say it's teaching: he did it so his community would. A version of the hadith says something covers my heart, a kind of cloud, and I ask forgiveness a hundred times a day. In Bukhari, the number is more than seventy. And it's not only about sins. Istighfar is also said at the end of the prayer, three times, right after the taslim, as if to say: I tried, and it wasn't perfect. The Qur'an adds a surprising promise. In Surah Nuh, the prophet Nuh tells his people: ask forgiveness of your Lord, and He will send rain, and help you with wealth and sons, and give you gardens and rivers. In that verse, asking forgiveness comes paired with rain. And there's a longer form, called the master of all istighfar, reported in Bukhari. But the short one, one word, is the one people carry all day.
screen: `GH-F-R — TO COVER, TO SHIELD.` · `WHY WOULD HE NEED IT?` · `THREE TIMES, AFTER THE PRAYER.` · `ASK, AND THE RAIN COMES.` · then, large: `A HUNDRED TIMES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a hundred on the fingers, or as many as fit. Rest your right hand, palm up. If you pray, say astaghfirullah on each finger joint, not rushing, and let a face or a moment come to mind now and then, something you'd like covered. If you don't, say sorry silently on each count, and mean some of them. You won't reach a hundred in two minutes if you go slowly; that's fine. Stop wherever the bell finds you. The bell holds the time.
Istighfar. Saying astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness; to be covered and shielded, a hundred times a day. Today's word.
Your line: I ask forgiveness. Today, trade one throwaway sorry for a real one, to someone who's owed it. Day one hundred eighteen.

screen: `DAY 118 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PRAYERS ON THE PROPHET ﷺ.`

119.title: Prayers on the Prophet ﷺ
119.hook: sending blessings on him, returned tenfold (Muslim)
119.howItsDone: Muslims say sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam whenever the Prophet is named, recite the prayer of blessings on Muhammad and Ibrahim in the last sitting of every prayer, and many increase their salawat on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: istighfar, astaghfirullah, to be covered and shielded. Your line was I ask forgiveness. Did you trade one throwaway sorry for a real one? Day one hundred nineteen.

A week on the fingers. The fingers that will testify. Glory, thirty-three. Praise, thirty-three. Greater, thirty-four, a gift to a tired daughter. No god but Allah, the card on the scale. Forgiveness, a hundred times. Every one of them about God. Today's is still addressed to God, but it asks for someone else, and you've been seeing it all along. Every time the Prophet's name has appeared on your screen on this path, it's been followed by a small symbol, a knot of Arabic calligraphy. Maybe you wondered what it was. Today: what that little symbol says.
screen: `A WEEK ON THE FINGERS.` → `A SMALL SYMBOL AFTER HIS NAME.` → `WHAT DOES IT SAY?`

segments.voice: The symbol is short for sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam: may Allah send blessings on him and peace. Saying it, or any prayer like it, is called salawat, the plural of salah, the same word as prayer. It's said when his name is spoken. Why? The Qur'an, in Surah al-Ahzab, says that Allah and His angels send blessings on the Prophet, and tells the believers: you, too, send blessings on him, and greet him with peace. So when a Muslim says it, they're joining something already happening. The companions took this seriously enough to ask how. A hadith in Bukhari says they came to him: we know how to greet you with peace, but how do we send blessings on you? And he taught them a prayer that begins, O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad and on the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings on Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. That's the prayer many Muslims recite in the last sitting of every prayer, just before the peace to both sides. Notice who's in it: Ibrahim, the friend of God, whose story you met in camp two. Then the promise that gives today its hook. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet said: whoever sends one blessing on me, Allah sends ten blessings on them. One goes out, ten come back. And the tradition has a gentle rebuke, too. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the stingy one is the person who hears my name and doesn't send a blessing. Stingy. Four words in Arabic, and holding them back earns that name.
screen: `SALLALLAHU 'ALAYHI WA SALLAM.` · `ALLAH AND HIS ANGELS SEND BLESSINGS.` · `AS YOU BLESSED IBRAHIM.` · `ONE GOES OUT, TEN COME BACK.` · then, large: `THE STINGY ONE HEARS AND IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ten salawat, slowly. Rest your right hand, palm up. If you pray, say on each count, sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam, or the longer prayer from the last sitting if you know it. Take your time; ten, not a hundred. If you don't, you can simply hold in mind the person the words are for, a man who, Muslims say, was sent as a mercy to the worlds, and count ten breaths. The bell holds the time.
Salawat. Blessings sent on the Prophet, the words behind the symbol; one sent, ten returned. Today's word, and a week of remembrance on your fingers.
Your line: peace on him. Every time you see that little symbol from now on, read it. Tomorrow, the path turns to a month: Ramadan, and the new moon. Day one hundred nineteen.
